newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Tight monetary policy to stay - S.Africa's Ramos.
newsitem.headline: Tight monetary policy to stay - S.Africa's Ramos.

text.p: South Africa was on track to meet its fiscal targets for 1996/97 (April-March), but monetary policy would remain tight until credit demand eased, Finance Director General Maria Ramos said on Wednesday.

Predicting that the government's macro-economic strategy for growth, employment and redistribution, known as GEAR, would soon begin to bear fruit, she said South Africa had to pursue sructural goals and not short-term returns.
"South Africans must get away from the view that you deal with a problem by simply throwing more money at it," she told a breakfast meeting of the Cape Town Press Club.

"For the current fiscal year, we are on target both on the revenue side and on the expenditure side, so we don't envisage that we will have to carry through any problems into the 97/98 budget from a fiscal deficit perspective," she said.

Ramos, in office since July, said the Finance Ministry was confident of reaching its 1996/97 targets, including economic growth of around three percent, a budget deficit of 5.1 percent of GDP and average inflation for 1996 of around eight percent.
She reaffirmed next year's March 12 budget would be based on a four percent deficit before borrowing, down from 6.4 percent in fiscal 1994/95.

"The planning is all around the four percent deficit, the one key element in the budget planning we are doing. And it is a composite deficit, not just of the national government, but across the board, including the provinces," she said.
She said anticipated revenue from the total or partial sale of state assets including the Telkom telecommunications corporation were not included in the deficit calculation.
The macro-economic blueprint commits the government to reduce the deficit to three percent by the end of the century, with growth up to six percent and job creation up to 400,000 a year.
Ramos said interest rates could not be forced down to artifically stimulate growth, but would have to come down as a result of fiscal and monetary policy.
"In addition to tightening the fiscal stance, the central bank continues to pursue a tight monetary policy.

"That monetary stance will remain until we see convincing evidence in this economy that consumption expenditure, the demand for credit, has declined, that the pressure on the money and capital markets has eased, that the liquidity constraint is not in the marketplace in the way that it is at the moment and that the balance of payments has started to react.
"Until that time, the monetary stance that is in place at the moment will be maintained," she said.
Ramos said consumer credit demand and the government's borrowing requirement were contributing to high interest rates, which could not be artificially manipulated.

"As we lift exchange controls, as foreign investments start coming in, as the economy starts growing, as the pressures of credit demand start easing, then we start creating the conditions for interest rates to respond in a positive manner by coming down," she said.
